<reason>The decisive fight was over whether a speed camera counts as "harsher post-crash penalty" machinery. B built its whole case on collapsing that distinction ("a camera without a penalty is a paperweight"), but A's rebuttal — that the motion targets harsher, post-crash, severity-based sanctions, whereas cameras are certainty-based, pre-crash, low-severity enforcement — held up under repeated pressure and was never squarely dismantled. A also converted B's strongest example (the reckless/impaired repeat driver) into a point for its own side by noting that narrowed lanes and speed tables constrain speed physically regardless of driver intent, whereas B's rebuttal (he'll "clip the planter" or hit something else) was comparatively weak against that physics-based claim. B's concession in A1 of Rebuttal 2 ("Yes, I'd fund the camera-and-20mph program") was honestly answered but tactically costly, and A exploited it cleanly in closing to argue the debate had essentially been conceded. B's counter-move on Houston/Oslo (arguing US penalties are underenforced) inadvertently reinforced A's certainty-over-severity thesis rather than rescuing B's position. B kept real pressure on throughout and its incapacitation and "90% unrebuilt grid" points were substantive, but A's closing more effectively crystallized why its mechanism reaches every trip, including the ones deterrence already failed on, giving it the cleaner path to the motion as worded.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's turn in Rebuttal 1/2 distinguishing pre-crash certainty-based camera enforcement from the motion's "harsher post-crash penalties," combined with flipping B's impaired-driver example into evidence for physical redesign, was the single most damaging and least-answered exchange of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
